title: The Total Landed Cost of Cross-Border Tokenized Capital
subtitle: FX quotation, slippage, prefunding, network charges and usable beneficiary proceeds
abstract: An apparently low-cost digital transfer can be expensive once acquisition, FX conversion, market depth, intermediary charges, regulatory processing, off-ramp and liquidity financing are included. This report proposes a corridor-level total-landed-cost framework for tokenized securities subscriptions, redemptions and cross-border value circulation. It distinguishes experimental route comparisons from measured market evidence.

evidence.heading: BIS research measures costs across complete routes
evidence.body: BIS Working Paper 1385, published October 2026, compares banks, fintech money-transfer operators and stablecoin rails using harmonized measures across currencies and transfer sizes. Its key design contribution for TSP-01 is a disciplined comparison of full payment paths instead of the cheapest step on any one rail. Crypto market settlement fees alone do not establish total beneficiary costs, and a fintech route may be more competitive in some corridors.

evidence.heading: FX liquidity and execution are separate from payment transport
evidence.body: Project Mariana experimentally tested automated market makers among hypothetical wholesale CBDCs, while Rialto examined FX-related frictions in cross-border retail payment settlement. These are useful architectures for liquidity discovery but do not imply that any particular stablecoin AMM provides deep, executable and regulated FX conversion in real capital-market corridors. Quote validity, balance-sheet inventory, settlement currencies and market access remain real constraints.

evidence.heading: Incomplete PvP exposes market participants
evidence.body: The BIS 2026 FX settlement risk research reviews exposures when one currency is irrevocably delivered without the other leg's delivery. Low quoted FX spreads do not compensate for an unmitigated principal loss in a default case. For a tokenized asset subscription, a currency conversion may be complete on one system while the securities acquisition is still pending; the liquidity and finality clocks must be tracked independently.

architecture.heading: Complete cost and outcome function
architecture.body: For notional N, compare a rate-adjusted output rather than simply sum nominal fees across currencies. A normalized approximation in basis points is TotalCost = FX spread + price impact + network/ramp fees + intermediary charges + financing cost + expected risk/failed-transfer cost. In absolute currency: N × (spread + slippage + funding-bps)/10,000 plus fixed fees. Use executable quotes at a given depth and a defined timestamp. A posted midpoint is not an executable price.

architecture.heading: Separate funding and liquidity provisioning
architecture.body: A financial institution can prefund a beneficiary account, borrow intraday liquidity, hold inventory of a settlement asset, or synchronize a delivery to reduce funding duration. Each changes capital occupancy and risk allocation. Measure maximum intraday cash reserved, average holding time, financing cost, failed-payment share and beneficiary credit time. A reduction in operational time does not imply a reduction in finality risk unless both legs' assurance improves.

architecture.heading: Route decisions depend on beneficiary context
architecture.body: The best route for a USD subscription into a regulated issuer may differ from the best method to return local-currency proceeds to investors. Some investor or recipient accounts cannot receive stablecoins or central bank money directly; a token-based intermediate settlement may require a licensed off-ramp. Compliance access, holiday calendars, provider concentration, refund routes and documented exception costs belong in the route score.

case.title: Synthetic three-rail comparison for USD 100,000
case.setup: Compare three illustrative transfer routes on a USD 100,000 notional. Figures are invented for method demonstration, not observed market pricing. Assume that each route is eligible, supports the required parties and settles the same net US-dollar economic obligation.
rows: No rail is cheapest by transfer fee alone
case.formula: Total landed cost ≈ N × ((spread_bps + slippage_bps + funding_bps)/10,000) + fixed charges. Digital example: 100,000 × (8+12)/10,000 + 0.40 + 20 = $220.40.
case.interpretation: Under these invented inputs the fintech transfer costs less than the digital-assisted route even though the digital network fee is only $0.40. Risk and elapsed time could still change route preference.

risks: Spot mid-rate is used as though a provider would fill USD 100,000 without price impact.
Quote depth and execution timestamp alongside every claimed result.
Provider advertises instant payment while its treasury reserves large idle balances.
FX spread, withdrawal and network fees counted in different currencies without conversion.
A normalized net-received-value model and source-of-rate evidence.
tests: Measure three live-test corridors using executable quotes at fixed ticket sizes and preserve provider, timestamp, funding and beneficiary assumptions.
Stress AMM depth by reducing liquidity and evaluating price impact alongside fixed provider quotes.
Compare synchronized and asynchronous payment legs with peak prefunding, beneficiary spendability and settlement risk as separate outputs.
conclusion: TLS should evaluate FX as a complete investment or return workflow, not a cheap network-transfer feature. The most useful measure is net spendable value at a verifiable settlement endpoint, accompanied by actual liquidity and risk requirements.

title: After-Hours Tokenized Securities: Basis, Market Makers and Liquidity Risk
subtitle: Why 24/7 receipt trading can deviate from an underlying exchange's last share price
abstract: A tokenized equity receipt may trade while its underlying share exchange is closed. Its price is then determined by executable demand, order-book depth, dealer inventory, reference-price expectations and redemption access—not by a live underlying market price. This report explains premiums, discounts, market-maker inventory responses and reopening gaps, and separates observed market prices from custody-backed entitlement.

evidence.heading: Fragmented trading hours create basis and valuation risks
evidence.body: The FSB's report on tokenisation highlights market fragmentation, valuation and liquidity concerns when the new market and reference market differ operationally. Token transfer capability at all hours does not provide a guaranteed two-sided market for the receipt, nor a way to sell or redeem the underlying at a fixed last-traded price. Asset and custody rights may be stable while a venue's market price changes considerably.

evidence.heading: Liquidity provision is a funded business
evidence.body: Market makers may hold token and underlying inventories, hedge via related instruments where permitted, or seek authorized creation and redemption to offset imbalances. An AMM substitutes pool mechanics for some quoting functions but remains exposed to inventory, price movements and adverse selection. Mariana demonstrates hypothetical wCBDC AMMs technically, not an assured securities-market arbitrage business. Neither mechanism guarantees a tokenized receipt will trade at its reference-equivalent price.

evidence.heading: Investor rights still depend on the securities structure
evidence.body: The SEC staff's tokenized securities statement distinguishes structures in which token buyers hold different legal claims. If an issuer-backed receipt is not freely redeemable into an underlying share, its market maker cannot rely on exact share-delivery arbitrage. If trading is restricted by eligibility or transfer-agent controls, a seeming basis opportunity may remain economically inaccessible to many investors.

architecture.heading: Define the reference-equivalent value
architecture.body: Let P be the reference share price in its local currency, FX the conversion into receipt quote currency and k the receipts per share. ReferenceEquivalent = P × FX / k, adjusted for differing dividends, fees or contract rights. Basis = (ReceiptPrice − ReferenceEquivalent) / ReferenceEquivalent. During an exchange closure P is stale; report its last update and distinguish an indicative fair value from official closing price and executable receipt prices.

architecture.heading: Dealer choice to buy or sell
architecture.body: If receipts trade at a premium, a dealer with lawful inventory and ability to create receipts might sell additional units against sufficient backing, subject to spread, borrowing and authorization. If receipts trade at a discount, a dealer able to redeem might purchase them and recover underlying value. Without those channels, price convergence may not occur. Inventory limits and exposure to reopening gaps can be more important than marginal network transfer costs.

architecture.heading: Market data and user protection
architecture.body: Show last-traded receipt price, executable bid and ask, displayed order-book depth, reference market close timestamp, conversion ratio, FX timestamp and a warning on unavailable redemption. A gap at next-day open changes mark-to-market portfolio value, not the quantity of receipts held. A dealer intervention changes price through executed supply and demand, not through a privileged authority to change the underlying reference security price.

case.title: Three synthetic overnight basis scenarios
case.setup: An underlying share closes at USD 245. Ten receipt units represent one share, giving USD 24.50 reference-equivalent per receipt at that moment; an off-hours receipt venue remains active.
rows: Dealer may sell authorized inventory; hedging and creation are not always accessible
Dealer may buy if redemption path and funding exist
Old receipt reference basis must be recalculated
Marked position $2,550 before any execution costs
Holder unit count remains 100; unrealized value changes with market price
case.formula: Basis_pre = (25.50 − 24.50) / 24.50 = 4.08%. If the underlying opens at $260 and receipt last remains $25.50, new indicative basis = (25.50 − 26.00)/26.00 = −1.92%.
case.interpretation: These are invented scenarios, not actual prices. Arbitrage depends on lawful issuance/redemption, market depth, spread, time, securities borrowing and settlement.

risks: App treats stale reference close as a continuously executable stock price.
Disclose reference timestamp and order-book depth.
Dealer 'makes liquidity' by minting receipts beyond custody backing.
Issuer authorization and real-time backing controls.
Dealer shorts premium receipts expecting convergence then underlying share opens much higher.
Inventory, scenario limits and funding stress tests.
tests: Simulate premium, discount, reopening-up and reopening-down cases with dealer inventory and a finite cash budget.
Measure spread and executable depth across hours; do not infer liquidity from transaction frequency alone.
Model a market maker unable to redeem due to bank holiday or corporate-action lock; test how basis persists.
conclusion: Tokenized securities can be technically transferable after hours without offering reference-price parity or guaranteed liquidity. TSR and TLS should provide transparent valuation, investor-rights disclosure and constrained market-making models rather than promise seamless arbitrage.
